question: The rating of a fuse or circuit breaker is chosen so that it protects:

options.text: The cable and the equipment it supplies, opening before either is overloaded
The load, by holding the voltage across it constant whatever the current
The pilot, by preventing any possibility of electric shock from the circuit
The generator only, by stopping it ever being loaded beyond its rating

explanation: A fuse or breaker is rated no lower than the circuit's normal current, but low enough to open before the current reaches the safe limit of the cable or the equipment on it. That is why only the specified rating may be fitted: a larger one lets a fault overheat the wiring or damage the load before it opens.

question: A fuse that has blown is replaced with one of a higher rating. The danger is that:

options.text: A fault could overheat the cable before the fuse melts, risking fire
The supply voltage to the circuit would rise above its normal value
The higher-rated fuse would blow immediately when the circuit is switched on
The circuit would no longer receive enough current to operate its load

explanation: The rating is chosen to protect that particular cable. A larger fuse lets a larger current flow indefinitely, so the wire, not the fuse, becomes the weakest link. Always replace a fuse with one of the same rating and type.

question: A fuse protects a circuit by:

options.text: A low-melting-point element melting on a sustained overcurrent
A coil pulling a set of contacts open whenever current flows in the wrong direction
A semiconductor junction blocking all current above a set voltage
A bimetal strip bending and pushing a trip button out when the current is too high

explanation: A fuse is a deliberately weak link: its element heats with I²R like the rest of the circuit but melts first, breaking the circuit permanently. It must then be replaced, unlike a circuit breaker which can be reset.

question: A current limiter, as fitted in heavy-current circuits such as generator feeders and bus ties, is:

options.text: A slow-blow copper-element fuse that rides out brief surges but opens on a sustained fault
A circuit breaker that can be reset from the cockpit after each overload
A resistor that holds the current at a fixed value whatever the load demands
A relay that opens whenever current flows back towards the generator from the bus

explanation: Heavy circuits see short, harmless surges — motor starting, for example. A current limiter's copper element has enough thermal mass to ride through those, while still melting on a sustained overload or short. Despite its name, it does not regulate current.

question: A thermal circuit breaker trips because:

options.text: A diode inside the breaker detects current flowing in the reverse direction
The voltage across the breaker rises above its rated value and arcs the contacts open
Excess current heats a bimetal, which bends and releases the contact latch
Excess current produces a magnetic field that pulls the contacts apart instantly

explanation: The bimetal responds to heating, so the trip time depends on both the size and the duration of the overload: a large overload trips it quickly, a small one more slowly. Magnetic breakers, by contrast, respond to current almost instantaneously.

question: A circuit breaker described as 'trip-free' is one which:

options.text: Never trips on a short circuit, only on a sustained overload
Will still trip on a fault even if its reset button is being held in
Is free of any thermal element, so it trips magnetically only
Can be reset any number of times without any delay between attempts

explanation: Trip-free means the mechanism cannot be overridden: the contacts open on a fault regardless of what is done to the button. Holding a breaker in cannot force current into a faulty circuit.

question: Compared with a thermal circuit breaker, a magnetic circuit breaker:

options.text: Trips only after the cable has reached a set temperature, however large the current
Trips almost instantly on a large fault, largely regardless of ambient temperature
Can be held closed against a fault by pressing and holding its button
Responds to the voltage across the circuit rather than to the current through it

explanation: A magnetic trip uses the field of the fault current itself to release the latch, so it is fast and independent of how warm the breaker is. Many breakers combine both: thermal for slow overloads, magnetic for short circuits.

question: A circuit breaker trips in flight. Unless the checklist directs otherwise, the generally accepted practice is to:

options.text: Reset it immediately and as many times as necessary until it stays in
Hold it in by hand so the system keeps working until landing
Replace it with a breaker of a higher rating taken from a less important circuit
Reset it once only, after allowing time for it to cool, and only if the system is needed

explanation: A trip means something drew too much current. One reset after a cooling period distinguishes a transient from a real fault; repeated resets push fault current into hot wiring and are a known cause of in-flight fires. Many operators prohibit resets of certain systems (fuel pumps, for example) altogether.

question: An advantage of circuit breakers over fuses in an aircraft is that circuit breakers:

options.text: Never need maintenance or replacement during the life of the aircraft
Protect the equipment as well as the wiring, so no internal fusing is needed
React faster than any fuse to every type of overload
Can be reset after tripping, and can be pulled manually to isolate a circuit

explanation: A breaker survives its own operation and doubles as an isolating switch — pulled (and sometimes collared) to make a circuit safe. A fuse must be replaced, which requires spares and access.

question: Arc-fault circuit breakers have been introduced in some modern aircraft because conventional thermal breakers:

options.text: Trip too readily on the normal starting currents of motors and pumps
Cannot be used on 28 V DC circuits at all, only on AC circuits
May miss intermittent arcing, as the average current stays below the trip level
Do not protect against a dead short between a conductor and the structure

explanation: An arc through chafed insulation produces short, erratic current spikes. Their heating effect may be too small for a bimetal to notice, yet the arc itself can ignite surrounding material. Arc-fault breakers recognise the current signature of arcing and open the circuit.

question: A reverse current circuit breaker (or cut-out) in a DC generating system is fitted to:

options.text: Limit the generator output current to its rated maximum
Disconnect the generator if current starts to flow back into it
Prevent the battery from being overcharged by the generator
Protect the bus wiring from short circuits between the generator and the battery

explanation: If a generator's voltage falls below the bus voltage (it slows down or fails), the battery and other generators would drive current back into it, motoring it and discharging the battery. Sensing that reversal and opening the line protects both.

question: A capacitor in a circuit stores energy:

options.text: As heat in a resistive element, released when the circuit is switched off
As chemical energy, converted back into electricity as it discharges
In the magnetic field around a coil of wire carrying current
In the electric field across the dielectric between two plates

explanation: Charging moves electrons onto one plate and off the other, leaving an electric field across the dielectric. Energy stored in a magnetic field describes an inductor; chemical storage describes a battery.

question: The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is increased by:

options.text: Replacing the dielectric with a material of lower permittivity
Increasing the plate area or reducing the distance between the plates
Increasing the voltage applied across the plates
Reducing the plate area or increasing the distance between the plates

explanation: Capacitance is proportional to plate area and to the permittivity of the dielectric, and inversely proportional to the plate separation. Voltage changes the charge stored (Q = CV), not the capacitance itself.

question: A 50 µF capacitor is charged to 28 V. What charge does it hold?

options.text: 14 mC
1.4 mC

explanation: Q = C × V = 50 × 10⁻⁶ F × 28 V = 1,400 × 10⁻⁶ C = 1.4 mC (millicoulombs).

question: Two 4 µF capacitors are connected in series. Their combined capacitance is:

options.text: 16 µF
4 µF
2 µF
8 µF

explanation: Capacitors combine the opposite way to resistors: in series, 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, so C = 2 µF. Connecting them in series effectively increases the plate separation.

question: Capacitors of 10 µF and 22 µF are connected in parallel. Their combined capacitance is:

options.text: 12 µF
6.9 µF
220 µF
32 µF

explanation: In parallel, capacitances simply add (C = C₁ + C₂), because the arrangement is equivalent to one capacitor with a larger plate area.

question: A capacitor charges through a resistor from a DC supply. After one time constant (CR seconds) the capacitor voltage has reached approximately:

options.text: 63% of the supply voltage
100% of the supply voltage
37% of the supply voltage
50% of the supply voltage

explanation: Charging is exponential: in each time constant the voltage covers 63% of the remaining gap to the supply. It is effectively fully charged (over 99%) after about five time constants. During discharge it falls to 37% in one time constant.

question: A 10 µF capacitor charges through a 100 kΩ resistor. The time constant of the circuit is:

options.text: 10 seconds
1 second
1 millisecond
0.1 second

explanation: τ = R × C = 100,000 Ω × 10 × 10⁻⁶ F = 1 s. The capacitor would be effectively fully charged after about 5 s.

question: Once a capacitor connected to a steady DC supply is fully charged, the current in its circuit is:

options.text: At its maximum, because the capacitor holds its maximum charge
Equal to the supply voltage divided by the series resistance
Alternating at a frequency set by the capacitance
Zero, because the capacitor voltage equals the supply voltage

explanation: Current flows only while the charge on the plates is changing. When the capacitor's voltage equals the supply's, there is no net voltage to drive current through the resistor, so a capacitor blocks steady DC.

question: Why must care be taken with large capacitors in equipment that has been switched off?

options.text: They generate a high-frequency voltage until they are manually earthed
They reverse polarity when switched off and can damage the supply
They can retain a dangerous charge for some time after the supply has been removed
They draw a large current from the supply even when the equipment is off

explanation: With no discharge path, a capacitor keeps its charge. Large capacitors in power supplies and some electronic units can deliver a dangerous shock long after switch-off, which is why they are fitted with bleed resistors and discharged before work starts.

question: An electrolytic capacitor differs from most other types in that it:

options.text: Is polarised, and connecting it the wrong way round can destroy it
Has a capacitance that rises sharply as the voltage across it increases
Stores its energy chemically, in the same way as a battery
Can be connected either way round and works equally well on AC and DC

explanation: An electrolytic capacitor achieves a high capacitance in a small package by using a very thin oxide film as its dielectric. That film is only maintained with the correct polarity; reverse voltage breaks it down and can make the capacitor overheat.

question: A capacitor is connected across the output of a rectifier. Its function is to:

options.text: Block the DC output so that only the alternating component reaches the load
Smooth the output, charging on each peak and feeding the load in between
Raise the DC output voltage to twice the peak value of the AC input
Limit the output current if the load is short-circuited

explanation: Rectified AC is a series of pulses. The capacitor fills during each peak and supplies the load in the troughs, so the output becomes a nearly steady DC with only a small ripple.

question: A capacitor of 100 µF is charged to 20 V. How much energy does it store?
explanation: Energy stored = ½CV² = 0.5 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 20² = 0.5 × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 400 = 0.02 J. Forgetting the half gives 0.04 J.

question: A circuit breaker panel has some breakers fitted with coloured collars. A collar is placed on a breaker to:

options.text: Mark breakers that protect AC circuits as opposed to DC circuits
Stop a deliberately pulled breaker being pushed back in by mistake
Show which breakers have tripped in flight and need resetting after landing
Increase the current rating of the breaker for heavy loads

explanation: When a system is made inoperative under a deferred-defect procedure, its breaker is pulled and collared so nobody inadvertently re-energises it. The collar is a physical lock-out, not an electrical device.

question: In flight a fuse blows. It is replaced once with one of the correct rating, and the new fuse blows as soon as the circuit is switched on. The correct action is to:

options.text: Fit a fuse of the next higher rating so the circuit can stay on
Bridge the fuse holder with wire until the aircraft has landed
Leave the circuit off: a second failure means a fault that must be found first
Keep replacing fuses of the correct rating until one holds

explanation: One replacement with the correct rating allows for a transient. If that blows too, there is a real defect in the system, and no further fuse should be fitted until the circuit has been investigated. A higher rating or a bridge would let the fault overheat the wiring.

question: Spare fuses must be carried on board. The usual minimum is:

options.text: None, since modern circuit breakers have replaced every fuse
One of each rating fitted, whatever the number installed
10% of the number of each rating fitted, with at least three of each
Half of the number of each rating fitted, with at least five of each

explanation: The rule ensures that every rating in use has replacements available in flight: ten per cent of each rating installed, but never fewer than three of any rating.

question: An important difference between a fuse and a circuit breaker is that:

options.text: A fuse can be reset after operating, while a breaker must be replaced
A fuse responds to excess voltage, while a breaker responds to excess current
A fuse usually opens before the full fault current is reached; a breaker opens after it
A breaker usually opens before the full fault current is reached; a fuse opens after it

explanation: A fuse element melts very quickly on a heavy fault and often interrupts it before the current has built up fully. A circuit breaker's mechanism takes slightly longer, so the breaker and the equipment it protects must both be able to withstand the full fault current for a short time.

question: A high rupture capacity (HRC) fuse differs from a glass cartridge fuse in that it:

options.text: Has a glass body, so the blown element can be seen without removing it
Is used for very small currents in instrument circuits
Can be reset by pressing a button once the fault has cleared
Has a ceramic body packed with sand or quartz, so it operates without flame

explanation: The robust ceramic body and filling of sand or powdered quartz quench the arc as the element melts. HRC fuses are used in high-current circuits; they act quickly and accurately, do not deteriorate with age and are little affected by ambient temperature.
